{{Short description|Random number generator}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=August 2025}}
[[File:Lava lamp wall at Cloudflare office -2.jpg|thumb|The Wall of Entropy is a wall of lava lamps at the San Francisco headquarters of [[Cloudflare]], which was inspired by Lavarand.]]

'''Lavarand''' is a [[hardware random number generator]] designed and trademarked by [[Silicon Graphics]] (SGI) in 1996.<ref name="patent">{{cite patent |country=US |number=5732138 |title=Method for seeding a pseudo-random number generator with a cryptographic hash of a digitization of a chaotic system |gdate=March 24, 1998 |fdate=February 29, 1996 |inventor1-last=Noll |inventor1-first=Landon Curt |inventor2-last=Mende |inventor2-first=Robert G. |inventor3-last=Sisodiya |inventor3-first=Sanjeev |assign1=Silicon Graphics, Inc.}}</ref><ref name="main_ref">{{cite web |url=https://www.sciencenews.org/article/lava-lamp-randomness |title=Lava Lamp Randomness |work=Science News |date=October 26, 2001 |access-date=August 20, 2025}}</ref> The system operates by digitizing the chaotic patterns of warm wax blobs oozing inside an array of [[lava lamp]]s. This data is then processed with a [[cryptographic hash function]] to produce a high-quality seed for a [[cryptographically-secure pseudorandom number generator]] (CSPRNG).<ref name="patent"/>

From 1997 to 2001, SGI ran a website that demonstrated the technology.<ref name="main_ref"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://lavarand.sgi.com/ |title=Welcome to Lavarand! |website=lavarand.sgi.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19971210213248/http://lavarand.sgi.com/ |archive-date=December 10, 1997 |url-status=dead |access-date=January 5, 2010}}</ref> Its visually distinct method made it a frequently cited example of entropy sourcing.<ref name="main_ref"/>

The concept was later revived and popularized by [[Cloudflare]], which uses a wall of lava lamps in its office lobby as one component of its entropy gathering system.<ref>{{cite web |last=Schwab |first=Katharine |date=August 18, 2017 |title=The Hardest Working Office Design In America Encrypts Your Data–With Lava Lamps |url=https://www.fastcompany.com/90137157/the-hardest-working-office-design-in-america-encrypts-your-data-with-lava-lamps |access-date=April 16, 2022 |website=Fast Company |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="cloudflare_chaos">{{cite web |url=https://blog.cloudflare.com/harnessing-office-chaos/ |title=Harnessing chaos in Cloudflare offices |work=The Cloudflare Blog |date=September 6, 2017 |access-date=August 20, 2025}}</ref>

==History==
SGI's invention of Lavarand was a direct response to a significant security crisis in the mid-1990s as the Internet was transitioning into a commercial platform.<ref name="tashian_history">{{cite web |url=https://tashian.com/articles/a-brief-history-of-random-numbers/ |title=A Brief History of Random Numbers |last=Tashian |first=Carl |date=January 14, 2015 |access-date=August 20, 2025}}</ref> The security of the new [[Secure Sockets Layer]] (SSL) protocol depended on high-quality random numbers for generating session keys. In 1995, computer science PhD students [[Ian Goldberg]] and [[David A. Wagner]] discovered that the implementation of SSL in [[Netscape Navigator]], the era's dominant [[web browser]], used a predictable method for seeding its pseudorandom number generator.<ref name="netscape-ssl-cracked">
{{cite newsgroup
| author = Ian Goldberg
| date = 1995-09-18
| title = Netscape SSL implementation cracked!
| newsgroup = hks.lists.cypherpunks
| url = http://www.cs.berkeley.edu/~daw/my-posts/netscape-cracked-0
| access-date = 2006-09-12
}}</ref> The seed was derived from the time of day, the process ID, and the [[parent process]] ID. An attacker could potentially guess these values, predict the seed, and compromise a secure session. This vulnerability highlighted the critical need for accessible and unpredictable sources of [[entropy]] to seed cryptographic systems.<ref name="tashian_history"/>

Lavarand was SGI's solution, invented and patented in 1996, the year after the Netscape vulnerability was exposed,<ref name="patent"/><ref name="main_ref"/> by mathematician and cryptologist [[Landon Curt Noll]], software engineer Robert G. Mende, and Sanjeev Sisodiya.<ref name="main_ref"/><ref name="patent"/> Noll was already known for his work on large prime numbers and for co-creating the [[Fowler–Noll–Vo hash function|Fowler-Noll-Vo (FNV) hash function]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.isthe.com/chongo/tech/comp/fnv/ |title=FNV Hash |website=www.isthe.com |author1=Fowler, Glenn |author2=Noll, Landon Curt |author3=Vo, Kiem-Phong |access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.cnet.com/tech/tech-industry/sgi-finds-prime-number/ |title=SGI finds prime number |first=Corey |last=Grice |date=February 24, 1998 |website=CNET News | url-status=dead | access-date=August 21, 2025}}</ref>

The system's hardware comprises an [[SGI O2]] [[workstation]], known for its multimedia capabilities; a proprietary SGI O2cam with a 512{{times}}480 pixel [[charge-coupled device|CCD]] sensor for image capture; and an array of six Lava Lite lamps as the chaotic source.<ref name="lavadiff">{{cite web |url=https://www.lavarand.org/news/lavadiff.html |title=Differences between SGI classic lavarand and our LavaRnd |access-date=August 20, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rainsbrook.co.uk/wiki/doku.php?id=rb:sgi-o2-webcam |title=rb:sgi-o2-webcam [Rainsbrook] |access-date=August 20, 2025}}</ref><ref name="patent"/> The process begins with the O2cam capturing a digital photograph of the lamps. This raw 921,600-byte image file, containing both the visual chaos of the wax and electronic noise from the camera's sensor, is then processed using the [[SHA-1]] hash algorithm to extract its unpredictability.<ref name="patent"/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://gist.github.com/UnquietCode/99b69b99e00ce52e34c1 |title=Lava Lamp Random Number Generator |work=GitHub Gist |access-date=August 20, 2025}}</ref> The hashing step produces a 140-byte hash output that is then used to seed a CSPRNG. The patent specifies the [[Blum Blum Shub]] generator as a preferred choice for the final stage, which can then produce a rapid stream of random numbers.<ref name="patent"/> The complete method was documented in {{US patent|5732138}}. The patent's claims are not limited to lava lamps but cover any chaotic system used in a similar manner, and its expiration allowed companies like Cloudflare to use the underlying concept without license.<ref name="main_ref"/><ref name="patent"/>

==Legacy==
Landon Curt Noll later collaborated with Simon Cooper to develop LavaRnd, an open-source successor designed to be more accessible and efficient.<ref name="lavadiff"/> LavaRnd differs from the original SGI system in several key areas. It replaces the visual entropy source of six lava lamps with the electronic thermal noise from a lens-capped webcam CCD.<ref name="wired_2003">{{cite news |url=https://www.wired.com/2003/08/random/ |magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] |title=Totally Random |volume=11 |issue=8 |date=August 2003}}</ref> A significant change is in its output; the SGI system produces a 140-byte seed for an external generator, but LavaRnd was designed to directly output a continuous stream of cryptographically sound random numbers. This redesign led to a major performance increase, from the SGI system's approximate 8,000 bits per second for seed generation to between 77,000 and 206,000 bits per second of random data from LavaRnd on a commodity PC of the era. The hardware requirements are democratized, moving from a specialized SGI O2 workstation to a standard PC and a low-cost webcam. Finally, the legal status changed from the proprietary SGI system covered by a U.S. Patent to LavaRnd's algorithm being placed entirely in the public domain.<ref name="lavadiff"/>

In 2017, the web infrastructure company [[Cloudflare]] launched its own entropy-gathering system, directly inspired by SGI's work.<ref name="cloudflare_chaos"/> The installation is located in the lobby of its San Francisco headquarters, with a wall of around 100 lava lamps that are continuously monitored by a camera.

Unlike the 1990s system, Cloudflare's Lavarand is not the primary source of entropy for its servers, because modern CPUs include their own high-speed hardware random number generators such as [[RDRAND]]. Instead, the data from the lava lamps is a secondary, independent source. The random data is made available to Cloudflare's global servers, which incorporate it into their local entropy pools to protect against any potential systemic flaws in the primary CPU-based generators.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.svbgroup.co.nz/insights/entropy |title=Demystifying Encryption and Entropy |work=Softsource vBridge |access-date=August 20, 2025}}</ref> Cloudflare has since expanded this concept into a global network of entropy sources, branded as the Wall of Entropy, to diversify its randomness inputs. Other installations include a wall of chaotic [[double pendulum]]s in its London office and a [[Geiger counter]] measuring the radioactive decay of a uranium pellet in its Singapore office.<ref name="cloudflare_chaos"/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://blog.cloudflare.com/lavarand-in-production-the-nitty-gritty-technical-details/ |title=LavaRand in Production: The Nitty-gritty Technical Details |work=The Cloudflare Blog |date=September 6, 2017 |access-date=August 20, 2025}}</ref>
